title: Delayed choice
seal: A decision made after the fact
reading: In 1978 John Wheeler, who will study with Professor Bohr in Copenhagen in the 1930s, proposes a variant of the two-slit experiment. Let a single light quantum enter an interferometer. Only after it has passed the point where it must 'decide' between one path or both, choose whether to measure which path it took, or to recombine the paths and observe interference. In 2007 the experiment is done with single light quanta at Cachan in France, the choice made by a random generator after the quantum has entered. The results agree with quantum mechanics: interference when the paths are recombined, which-path information when they are not — regardless of when the choice is made.
detail: Wheeler framed the result in Bohr's terms: 'no elementary phenomenon is a phenomenon until it is a registered phenomenon'. Nothing is sent backwards in time; the statistics never allow signalling. Quantum-eraser variants (from 1999) extend the idea using entangled pairs.

claim.label: Only the registered phenomenon
claim.summary: Wheeler explicitly framed the experiment in Bohr's language. Bohr died before it was proposed; his reaction is inferred from complementarity.
voice: There is no paradox, provided we do not ask what the quantum 'did' before the arrangement was complete. A phenomenon is defined by the whole experimental arrangement, including the last choice. Until it is registered, there is no phenomenon to have happened one way or the other.
claim.reasoning: Complementarity applies to completed arrangements, not partial histories.

claim.label: What did it do in between?
voice: Bohr's answer is always that we must not ask. I will ask anyway. When the quantum was inside the apparatus, before anyone chose, what was it doing? If physics cannot say, then physics is not finished.
claim.reasoning: A real state at every time.

claim.label: The path arises when observed
voice: This is my sentence about the path, tested in time. The path comes into existence only when we observe it — and apparently it does not mind when we decide to observe it.

claim.label: The particle took one path
claim.summary: In pilot-wave theory the particle always follows one path and the wave explores both; the delayed choice affects which detector the guided particle reaches, with no retrocausation. Attributing this analysis to de Broglie is inference.
voice: In my picture there is nothing mysterious. The particle went one way; the wave went both. What the last choice changes is how the wave recombines, and therefore where it guides the particle. Nothing reaches into the past.
